hook_text: On 21 March 1960, people walked to a police station without their passes, and in forty seconds, South Africa changed forever.
clip_script: Sharpeville, 21 March 1960. Thousands of people gather at the police station. They have left their pass books at home. Arrest us, they say. They sing. They wait. Armoured cars arrive. Jets scream overhead. Just after one o'clock, there is pushing at the gate. Then the police open fire. No warning. Forty seconds. Sixty-nine people are dead, many shot in the back as they ran. In Cape Town, a young student leads thirty thousand people on a peaceful march into the city, and is arrested after sending them home. The government declares a state of emergency and bans the ANC and PAC. Peaceful protest has been met with bullets, and the struggle will never be the same again. Today, 21 March is Human Rights Day.
visual_style: Black-and-white photos of the crowd outside Sharpeville police station; Saracen armoured cars; jets flying low; people running across open ground; a memorial with names of the dead; the Langa march filling a Cape Town street; Mandela signing the Constitution at Sharpeville in 1996.
pacing: Calm at first, sudden silence at the shooting, slow and heavy afterwards.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to understand the causes and consequences of Sharpeville and the Langa march.
